findings.claim: Justin's description is quoted only for its order; the same chapter says the presider prays 'according to his ability', the free-worship side's favorite second-century datum, and the line should carry both.
findings.evidence: Justin, First Apology 67 (also 65): the president 'offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability' (ὅση δύναμις αὐτῷ); Bradshaw, The Search for the Origins of Christian Worship, on improvised presidential prayer.
findings.fix: {when: 'c. 155', what: 'Justin Martyr\'s First Apology 67: Sunday readings, a sermon, prayers, and the Eucharist, the presider giving thanks "according to his ability".'}

findings.claim: The liturgical side jumps from Justin (155) to Cranmer (1549), so the first named liturgy in the list is Anglican; the liturgies celebrated every Sunday by the Orthodox Church, coordinated at worship 5, do not appear.
findings.evidence: The Liturgy of St Basil (4th c., Cappadocia) and the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom (Antioch/Constantinople, 4th-5th c.) are the ordinary eucharistic rites of Orthodoxy and the oldest liturgies in continuous use.
findings.fix: Insert after Justin: {"when": "4th-5th c.", "what": "The Liturgies of St Basil and St John Chrysostom take the shape still celebrated every Sunday in the Orthodox Church."}
